issues.legal_issue: Only the drawer of a dishonoured cheque may be prosecuted for the offence of cheque dishonour, and a joint account holder who did not sign the cheque is not liable merely because the account is jointly held.
material_facts: The cheque was drawn on a joint account, but only the other account holder signed it.
The appellant was named in the complaint but had not signed the cheque.
The complaint was brought for cheque dishonour, and the appellant sought to quash the proceedings against her.
issues.conclusion: The appellant, as a non-signatory joint account holder and not the drawer, could not be prosecuted for cheque dishonour; the proceedings against her were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes the drawer liable when its cumulative requirements are met. The Court relied on Jugesh Sehgal v. Shamsher Singh Gogi for those requirements and the need for the accused to have drawn the cheque. Penal statutes are strictly construed, and criminal law does not impose vicarious liability without specific statutory authority: S.K. Alagh v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Sham Sunder v. State of Haryana. Section 141 provides a specific exception for liability connected with an offence committed by a company, but did not apply to these facts. The Court endorsed the approach in Devendra Pundir v. Rajendra Prasad Maurya, Gita Berry v. Genesis Educational Foundation, and Smt. Bandeep Kaur v. S. Avneet Singh.

rule.if: criminal_cheque_dishonour_proceeding and accused_is_joint_account_holder and cheque_was_drawn_on_joint_account and not accused_signed_cheque

predicates.criminal_cheque_dishonour_proceeding: A criminal proceeding was brought for the dishonour of a cheque.
predicates.accused_is_joint_account_holder: The accused was one of the holders of the account on which the cheque was drawn.
predicates.cheque_was_drawn_on_joint_account: The cheque was drawn on an account held jointly by the accused and another person.

issues.definition: When a criminal cheque-dishonour proceeding concerns a cheque drawn on a joint account and the accused joint account holder did not sign it, that holder is not prosecutable as the drawer.

issues.legal_issue: A person cannot be prosecuted as part of an association of individuals on a theory of liability connected with a company where the complaint did not allege that basis of liability.
material_facts: The complainant argued that the accused and her husband could be treated as an association of individuals and that liability could therefore extend to her.
The complaint did not allege that the accused was being prosecuted as part of an association of individuals.
issues.conclusion: The association-of-individuals argument was rejected because it had not been raised in the complaint; the expression was to be interpreted in light of the purpose of the statutory vicarious-liability scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 creates specific vicarious liability in defined circumstances. The Court held that the terms relating to an association of individuals had to be construed ejusdem generis in light of that purpose, referring to Raghu Lakshminarayanan v. Fine Tubes. The Court also rejected reliance on Section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 to establish the proposed basis of prosecution where it had not been alleged in the complaint.

predicates.criminal_cheque_dishonour_proceeding: A criminal proceeding was brought for the dishonour of a cheque.
predicates.complaint_did_not_allege_accused_as_asso: The complaint did not allege that the accused was being prosecuted as part of an association of individuals.
predicates.association_liability_raised_only_later: The complainant first relied on liability based on an association of individuals after the complaint had been filed.

issues.definition: If a complaint does not allege that the accused is being prosecuted as part of an association of individuals, a later reliance on that basis does not make that liability available.

issues.legal_issue: A request to quash criminal proceedings cannot be refused merely because the trial is said to be in progress when the proceedings are not at an advanced stage and the accused raises a legally sustainable ground for quashing.
material_facts: The accused sought to quash the process issued against her and the criminal proceedings.
The High Court declined to quash the proceedings partly on the basis that the trial had commenced.
The Magistrate had directed the parties to address the admission or denial of documents, and the proceedings were not at an advanced stage.
The accused was not the signatory or drawer of the cheque.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to refuse to consider quashing on the ground that the trial was in progress; the proceedings were quashed against the accused.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a person may approach the High Court to seek quashing after process has issued. It found that the proceedings were not at an advanced stage and that the accused had a valid ground for quashing because she was not the drawer. The quashing jurisdiction invoked was under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

rule.if: petition_to_quash_criminal_proceeding and process_has_been_issued and trial_not_at_advanced_stage and accused_is_not_drawer

predicates.petition_to_quash_criminal_proceeding: The accused filed a petition seeking to quash a criminal proceeding.
predicates.process_has_been_issued: A court had issued process against the accused.
predicates.trial_not_at_advanced_stage: The trial had not progressed beyond preliminary procedural steps.
predicates.accused_is_not_drawer: The accused did not draw the cheque.

issues.definition: When an accused seeks to quash proceedings after process has issued, the trial is not advanced, and the accused is not the drawer, the proceedings are quashed against that accused.

issues.legal_issue: An objection that an applicant suppressed material facts does not justify rejecting the applicant's challenge where the relevant materials for deciding it were placed before the court.
material_facts: The appellant attached the statutory notice, the reply, the complaint, and the order issuing process to her challenge.
The respondent argued that the appellant had suppressed material facts about her involvement in the transaction.
The Court considered the attached materials relevant to deciding the complaint for cheque dishonour.
issues.conclusion: The suppression objection was rejected because the appellant had provided the materials relevant to the challenge.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the relevant materials for considering a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 had been annexed, so the allegation of suppression could not defeat the challenge. It found the authorities relied on by the respondent—Oswal Fats and Oils Limited v. Additional Commissioner (Administration), Balwantrai Chimanlal Trivedi v. M.N. Nagrashna, and J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao—inapplicable to these facts.

predicates.applicant_challenged_criminal_cheque_dis: The applicant challenged a criminal proceeding for the dishonour of a cheque.
predicates.applicant_provided_relevant_complaint_ma: The applicant placed before the court the materials relevant to deciding the challenge.
predicates.opposing_party_alleged_suppression: The opposing party argued that the applicant had concealed material facts.

issues.definition: When an applicant provides the materials relevant to a challenge to a criminal cheque-dishonour proceeding, an allegation of suppression does not defeat the challenge.
